messages.subject: Re: ggplot2 premium services survey report
parts:
On 2012-Mar-19, at 16:08 , Hadley Wickham wrote:
>
> I've attached the results of last weeks survey on premium services,
> with a bit more context about why I'm thinking about it. Please use
> this email thread for any questions, discussion etc.

From your write up, I conclude that ggplot2 membership and premium support should be two separate things:

- the membership could resemble that of many other scientific societies:
. a yearly fee of $20-30, which people pay to signify their interest in the subject, to support ggplot. If you can reward donators with cheap/free memorabilia, that's even better. Ideas: a t-shirt, a mug, an acknowledgment on the website (for those who want it), the right to add "I am a ggplot supporter" message in their email signature, a badge on their website, a newsletter that you (and/or others) would edit with "the best of ggplot on the web" etc.
. additional fees for more expensive goods, such as a (signed) copy of the book (in other societies, this is typically journal subscriptions)

- the premium support system could be on a subscription or time-billing basis and would work as any other consultancy work would.
You would have to figure out a good business strategy to make this work of course, but something based on increasingly expensive plans such as :
. free : the ggplot mailing list !
. 50$ a year : 15 premium-support emails
. 100$ a year : 30 premium-support emails or skype calls, discount on 1 online course
etc.
is common with web services and easily grasped by most people.


I think these two items should be kept separate because they target different people and would be paid with different sources of money. The membership would probably interest most people on this mailing list and would be paid with personal money. The premium support targets very specific needs (some of which you highlight in the document you sent) and would probably be paid with company money.

That's just the opinion of a future ggplot membership subscriber of course ;)

Jean-Olivier Irisson

messages.author: a3c668b849637905
messages.subject: Re: ggplot2 premium services survey report
parts:
Hi,

I have some reservations on the premium support idea.

It may be that the way ggplot2's help and development work now --
organically driven by enthusiasts from this list, R-help, SO, github
-- are already close to optimal (a trade-off between how many hours
dedicated but busy people are willing to spend on it, and the quality
of the contributions).
Charging for some select answers would certainly alter that delicate
balance. For one thing, if one pays for an answer, one should expect
an authoritative one. But these can often only come from a handful of
people, and their professional consulting rate would be very high as
you point out.

I don't know what motivates us folks to answer currently; it's
probably a variable mix of reasons, from improving your online
reputation, learning, entertainment, killing time, showing off,
curiosity, urge to teach things, genuine help, etc. It could be argued
that raising money would never work as well as an incentive, and could
also have detrimental effects on the personal drive of some list
members.

Are there examples of open-source communities that have set up a
successful premium membership? Maybe we can learn from their story.

If money can speed up the development of ggplot2, I think the other
options (t-shirts, books, donations) are much less interfering; in
this regard would it not be an option to simply add a line to the
ggplot2 mailing list signature saying that donations are welcome?

Just my 2 cents

Cheers,

baptiste

parts:
In ggplot2 0.89 plotmatrix would give a scatter plot matrix with that was correctly individualized for the rows, as in the attached plot done with the earlier version of ggplot2 (Fig1 ggplot2 0.89.jpg). Using the same code with ggplot2 version 0.9 gives an incorrect plot (Fig1 ggplot2 0.89.jpg). I'm teaching an in-house short course on ggplot2 using version 0.9 next week, so any help would be greatly appreciated.


# Fig. 1
# correlation matrix for 5 column data.frame
# use theme for faceted plot!

# create data
v1 <- rnorm(100)
v2 <- 10 + .5*v1 + rnorm(100)/2
v3 <- -3 + -7*v1 + 2*rnorm(100)
v4 <- 1 + .5*v1 + rnorm(100)/2
d4 <- data.frame(v1, v2, v3, v4)

library(ggplot2)
theme2 <- theme_update(
panel.grid.minor = theme_blank(),
panel.grid.major = theme_blank(),
panel.background = theme_blank(),
panel.border = theme_rect(linetype="solid"),
axis.line = theme_segment(),
axis.text.x = theme_text (colour="black", hjust = 0.5, vjust = 1),
axis.text.y = theme_text (colour="black", hjust = 1, vjust = 0.5)
)
plotmatrix(d4) + geom_smooth(method="lm")

messages.author: c55591d2e988ddca
messages.subject: Re: ggplot2 premium services survey report
parts: On 03/20/2012 05:10 AM, Jean-Olivier Irisson wrote:

> I agree that the paid support could discourage those who basically
> do it for free right now. I personally consider the time spend
> answering questions as a way to "pay" for this otherwise free bounty
> that is ggplot (and I don't do it as often as I should given this
> standard) but it's difficult to know the motivation of everyone
> indeed.

There's significant research on this topic. I recommend 'Predictably
Irrational', by Dan Ariely, as a readable sketch, aimed at the general
public but reasonably detailed.

The bit most relevant to this conversation is "The Cost of Social
Norms -- Why we are happy to do things, but not when we are paid to do
them." The key points might be phrased something like this:


+ It's easy to move an individual from viewing behavior as "social" to
seeing it as participation in a "market".

+ It's difficult to move the other way, from market-encourage behavior
to socially-encouraged; it's also difficult to maintain both
motivations simultaneously.

+ Market behavior outcompetes social behavior in a community.


To quote:

"When a social norm collides with a market norm, the social norm goes
away for a long time. In other words, social relationships are not
easy to reestablish. Once a social norm is trumped by a market norm,
it will rarely return."


I'm not (quite) speaking against paid support; I'm more pointing out
the mental pitfalls to which people are heir, once they start
accepting pay for behavior they were once proud to do for free as a
social duty.

Hadley's manner towards his community is IMO nearly a textbook for
managing such behavior; he pushes credit out to the community. Other
humans who hope to get some regular market reinforcement from ggplot2
ought to follow his example and keep an eye on their attitudes; The
market tendencies are written deep in our genes in many ways.


- Allen S. Rout

Hello,

The data look the same; I think the problem is that the x and y axes scales in Fig1 ggplot2 0.9.jpg are fixed/normalized whereas they are freescale in Fig1 ggplot2 0.89.jpg.  You may have load/require the scales package (which is no longer auto loaded with ggplot2 in v0.9) and set the axes to freescale.

The suggestion about pay for answers will not substitute the ggplot2 list in my point of view.

I'm very new with ggplot2 and this list, but on those some months I had seen some amount of messages of users who just want to create some nice-looking graphs, and had just landed on the R and ggplot world, having basic primary questions about ggplot2 and R itself.

The paid system could aim this kind of user, where the time to see the graph working is important enough to pay for, and the study and comprehension of ggplot and R can come later.

With this, the workflow will be answer first the pending "paid" questions, offering a complete full solution covering ggplot2 and R code, and after keep helping on the "open" list.

Complete full solution on the "open" list will not disappear, will just take some more time to shows up, because the "priority" of the paid questions.

And a suggestions: the paid solutions could be later accessible to everyone in the form of tutorials or something like. What do you think?

messages.author: 85d768b545989d80
messages.subject: Re: ggplot2 premium services survey report
parts:
Hi,

Some thoughts....

Working in a big company, I can easily get for example USD900 for something that make sense to the company. It could be a file-area with all ggplot-material in one place, perhaps in the form of blog. I could argue that even if all the material is available on internet, I would save time. The ggplot book could be stored there too. This would be a voluntary model adapted to companies. I understand that T-shirts or cups are interesting, but in a corporate environments it can be difficult to ask for that. But to say "give me USD900 so I can save 10 hours per week" make sense to some managers. Honestly, at times I find it difficult to keep up with all great stuff people write about ggplot and R on blogs and forums, to have a structured place of getting the newest and best info, even if it is just links to open web-pages, would help a lot.

Best regards,
/Chris

On Wed, Mar 21, 2012 at 12:03 PM, Bruce Raup <bruc...@gmail.com> wrote:
I throw my voice to the voluntary donation model.  Perhaps the
Wikipedia model would be better than the NPR one, but a cool ggplot2
gear store, and a simple way to donate on the website would probably
go a long way toward raising the revenue you're needing. --Bruce Raup
